So those that mean the U.S. Econamany is almost completely dependent on other nations?
No, that would be the import numbers. And we're not so much dependent as interdependent.

We expert a lot and we also import a lot. Much of what we export is services and highly complex and expensive capital (e.g. mining & farm equipment). Much of what we import is simple and cheap consumer goods. We do spend more on imports than we earn from exports, but the common reference point of "you go to the store and it's impossible to find things made in America!" is not an accurate representation of how trade works.

The "almost completely dependent on other nations" statement is just protectionist rhetoric because it intentionally overlooks the fact that a transaction is mutually beneficial. Is a customer more dependent on a factory than the factory is on its customers? Consider if the US stops buying plastic laundry baskets from foreign countries and reuses old cardboard boxes instead, vs if foreign countries refuse to sell us plastic laundry baskets so Americans have to make due with an inferior substitute - reused cardboard boxes. Alternatively, some may spend more money to acquire something of utility equal to the plastic basket. The end result in both circumstances is that the Americans have more money but have to dick around with cardboard boxes and loses the utility from using a superior substitute, or have less money but are no better off utility-wise. Meanwhile foreigners have a huge surplus of plastic laundry baskets and have to slash prices in order to sell them, eventually some of those factories will close and workers will be laid off. Who was more dependent? Regardless of who selected the change in the trade arrangement, the outcome was the same and left both parties worse off.

That's an oversimplification and there are circumstances and types of goods where this example would not be relevant, but looking only at trade #'s and making sweeping declarations about what those numbers mean and if they're good/bad is also an oversimplification
